name: The Dunning-Kruger Effect
statement: The least skilled are said to be too unskilled to see how unskilled they are.
statementAccent: too unskilled to see how unskilled they are
meaning: In its original claim, people who perform poorly at a task tend to overestimate their ability at it, showing a large gap between how well they think they did and how well they actually did. The proposed reason is metacognitive: the skills needed to do a task well are much the same as those needed to recognise doing it badly, so the least competent are least able to see their own incompetence. The popular one-liner — the incompetent are too incompetent to know it — is a compression that overstates the underlying data.
mechanism: Kruger and Dunning had Cornell students take tests of humour, logical reasoning, and grammar, then estimate their own rank against peers. Sorted into quartiles by actual score, the bottom quartile scored near the twelfth percentile yet rated themselves around the sixty-second — a gulf of some fifty points. The chart is symmetric in a less-noticed way: top performers slightly underestimated their rank, which the authors put down to wrongly assuming the task was as easy for others. But a powerful statistical critique holds that much of this pattern is built into the method rather than a fact about minds.

examples.text: Across humour, logic, and grammar, the worst-scoring quarter of students placed themselves far above their true rank, the finding that launched the effect.

Most people rate themselves above the median on common skills — famously, a large majority of drivers call themselves better than average, which cannot be true for more than half — a related upward bias that helps produce the pattern.
The internet curve of a confidence peak crashing into a valley of despair is folk elaboration, not from the 1999 paper, whose self-ratings run roughly flat with no such peak.

variants.name: The autocorrelation critique
variants.text: Because the chart plots self-assessment minus performance against performance, the same score sits on both axes, so the two are bound to correlate negatively; feeding pure random numbers through the method reproduces the famous figure.

variants.name: The regression-to-the-mean account
variants.text: Sorting people by a noisy score and then reading a second noisy measure makes the extreme groups' second measure drift toward the average, manufacturing apparent over- and under-estimation with no psychological effect at all.

whyItMatters: It became one of the most cited ideas in popular psychology, a byword for the blindness of the incompetent. Its later history is just as instructive: it has become a case study in how a compelling chart can encode a statistical artefact, and in how hard it is to separate a real cognitive effect from the mathematics of the measurement — a caution worth as much as the original claim.

working.text: treat self-assessments of skill with caution, since calibration between felt and actual competence is often poor, especially at the low end.
prefer objective tests and outside feedback over self-report when judging ability, your own included.
cite the phenomenon knowing its magnitude is disputed and much of the classic pattern may be a statistical artefact.

limits: The status of the effect is genuinely contested. A strong methodological literature argues the signature chart is largely, and perhaps entirely, a product of two artefacts: autocorrelation, since performance appears on both axes, and regression to the mean acting on noisy scores, together with the general better-than-average bias. Reanalyses using continuous methods rather than the quartile chart find misprediction roughly equal across the whole ability range and conclude any real asymmetric effect is far smaller than first claimed. But it is not simply debunked: defenders, Dunning among them, hold that a residual effect survives, and the critiques have themselves been challenged. The honest verdict is that the evidence is badly confounded and the question open.
misreadings: The data do not show that low performers are more confident than high performers in absolute terms — the bottom quartile still rated themselves below the top quartile, just not low enough; the effect is about miscalibration, not a confidence inversion. And it is not a settled law of psychology but a contested finding whose famous chart may be mostly an artefact of how the numbers are plotted.
origin: Introduced by Justin Kruger and David Dunning in 'Unskilled and Unaware of It' (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1999), which won a 2000 Ig Nobel Prize; the statistical-artefact critiques came chiefly from Nuhfer and colleagues (2016-2017) and Gignac and Zajenkowski (2020), and the debate continues.

sources.text: Kruger & Dunning, "Unskilled and Unaware of It," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 77(6):1121-1134 (1999). — the original studies and the metacognitive claim.
Gignac & Zajenkowski, "The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact," Intelligence 80 (2020). — continuous-method reanalysis finding misprediction roughly equal across ability.
Nuhfer et al., "Random Number Simulations Reveal How Random Noise Affects the Measurements... of Self-Assessed Competency," Numeracy 9(1) (2016). — the noise-and-graphing-convention critique.
